hero.title: Toll Brothers Homebuying AI Chatbot
hero.subtitle: Designing context-awareness, category recommendations, and home comparison

sections.intro: I led design for Toll Brothers' first AI chatbot and shaped three features. The core context system allows the user to build up common context of homebuying criteria (location, price, beds, etc.) with suggested replies. The category cards with nested product recommendations surfaces key marketing terms. The comparison feature leverages AI capbilitiies to summarize qualitative and quantitative differences between home choices. The context system and category cards was approved for implementation by internal stakeholders. The comparison feature was scoped for a future release.
Many commercial chatbots deliver underwhelming experiences. To understand good AI experiences, I analyzed several consumer-focused chatbots.

items: (Luxury Space) BMW - The flow centers on specific models and preferences and doesn't offer suggestions for broader category search.
(Homebuilder) Lennar - The flow carried context decently well but generally lacks visuals and suggested prompts.
(Ecommerce) Sephora and Amazon - Similar experiences with sophisticated continuous suggestions built around SKUs with visuals. The chat also updates on navigation to a product page.

blocks.text: The best chatbot experiences are able to retain multiple contexts and offer intersectional recommendations.

sections.intro: Working with the creative director, I distilled insights from the competitive analysis and shaped them into two broad requirements for an MVP. Since homebuyers tend to have predictable concerns, the chatbot's prompts should guide basic questioning around those topics. The second requirement was to generate content that could not be easily replicated on the site.

I first designed the initial flow around suggested prompts and demonstrated how the responses build context. I explained the concept that each suggested prompt adds a block of context that shapes the outcome of the chat. I made a key decision to lean away from direct product recommendations and designed the collapsible Category Cards for three reasons:

items: Product recommendations are visually noisy and will greatly extend the chat. Just 2 context blocks are not enough to accurately recommend a luxury home.
Category recommendations present more specific homebuying parameters like single-family, townhomes, or marketing terms like Active Adult (55+) to spark further discussion.
The category cards can recommend either homes or communities, depending on the blocks given (e.g., a timeframe block is more likely to surface a Quick Move-In Home category).

figures.caption: Introduction and suggested options representing the 5 main context blocks (Location, Timeframe, Price, Size, Amenities) for homebuying as well as brand promotion and contacting Sales.

User chooses the location context and chatbot asks for location refinement, with predictive suggestions based on user behavior on site. I proposed pinning the last user response to the top, allowing users to recall their input and adjust if necessary.

If location is the only block, the user is shown Category Cards showcasing product offerings specific to that region. (The faded option up top is for demonstration purposes and will not show up in the actual experience.)

If the user attempts to first input a block that is not location, their initial preference is noted and the chatbot immediately asks for location afterwards. The resulting Category Cards reflect the initial block selected.

sections.header: Product Flow and Product Comparison Feature
sections.intro:
Once the user clicks on a recommendation, there are two possible interactions. The chatbot can generate information inline, or the user is linked to the specific product page while the chatbot provides contextual prompts. The second option presents a novel experience where the chatbot supplements the product page. However, this idea was shelved given that our product pages are not designed with a persistent chatbot in mind, and the benefit is limited on mobile viewports. So, I went with Option 1 and designed a smaller summary of the main product page.

Here, I highlighted the Home Comparison feature. Users can ask for a home comparison summary through a simple prompt. This idea was well received and has been scoped for a future release.

figures.caption: Instead of linking to the specific product page, users are given a summarized version of the product page that is tailored to context blocks.
I suggested the Product Comparison feature to take advantage of AI's capabilities to analyze a matrix of data and provide qualitative assessments in natural language.
I designed a toggle for the user to choose between natural language summaries and explicit data points.
The current site can't visualize two floor plans side-by-side. This provides a method of seeing a side-by-side comparison.

sections.intro: This project had several branching design possibilities, and through a series of feedback sessions with stakeholders, we arrived at a thoughtful, refined MVP design for an AI-powered homebuying chatbot. The prototype was internally tested and approved for production with the main goal of gathering data on user responses. For future considerations, I advocated for the home comparison summary feature as well as tools that help describe surrounding areas. I also presented designs for embedded AI features as future possibilities.
